triage.name: Neonatal abstinence syndrome
triage.reason: Infant with irritability, high-pitched cry, tremor and feeding problems whose mother used opioids in pregnancy; diagnosis is clinical from maternal and infant history.

Late-term or high-dose maternal opioid exposure

chief_complaints.text: My baby won't stop crying and seems very jittery
She is not feeding well and is spitting up
He is not sleeping and is very irritable

hpi.onset: Symptoms begin after birth, typically within 24–72 hours for short-acting opioids and up to 5–7 days for methadone or buprenorphine
hpi.duration: Days to weeks; may persist for several weeks if untreated
hpi.progression: Symptoms appear and worsen over the first few days of life, peak, then gradually improve with supportive care and treatment
hpi.location: Generalized; involves the central nervous system, gastrointestinal tract, and autonomic system
hpi.quality: Irritability, high-pitched cry, tremors, increased tone, feeding difficulties, loose stools
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; severity varies with the substance, dose, timing of last exposure, and infant factors
hpi.timing: Continuous or episodic; worse with handling and feeding

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm infants may show less severe withdrawal with fewer gastrointestinal symptoms and more subtle neurologic signs; symptoms may be delayed.
Infants exposed to benzodiazepines or barbiturates may have a later onset and more seizures.

general.mild: Alert, consolable with swaddling and feeding; mild jitteriness when handled
general.moderate: Irritable and difficult to console; high-pitched cry; tremors and increased tone with handling
general.severe: Markedly irritable, inconsolable, continuous high-pitched cry; hypertonia, exaggerated reflexes, feeding poorly
general.critical: Exhausted or lethargic between episodes of extreme irritability; poor feeding, dehydration, possible seizures

labs.caveat: Hypoglycemia is a treatable mimic of withdrawal; check glucose in any irritable, jittery, poorly feeding newborn before attributing symptoms to withdrawal.
Hyponatremia from poor intake, vomiting and diarrhea; can itself cause irritability, lethargy or seizures.
Low bicarbonate reflects dehydration and metabolic acidosis from poor feeding and diarrhea.
Elevated from dehydration and poor intake; a normal BUN does not exclude significant fluid loss.
Neonatal creatinine is normally higher than in older children and falls over the first days of life; interpret against the infant's age and trend.
Hypocalcemia is a classic mimic of neonatal withdrawal and can cause jitteriness, tremor and seizures; check ionized calcium if total calcium is borderline.
Hypomagnesemia often accompanies hypocalcemia and can perpetuate jitteriness and seizures.
Neonatal TSH is normally higher than in older children and is usually screened on the newborn blood spot; overt hypothyroidism is a rare mimic of poor feeding and lethargy.

imaging.preferred_when: Infant with seizures, abnormal neurologic exam, or suspected intracranial hemorrhage; avoids radiation

findings.text: Normal brain parenchyma and no intraventricular or parenchymal hemorrhage

imaging.preferred_when: Seizures or focal neurologic findings not explained by ultrasound; better characterization of subtle injury
Suspected obstruction, necrotizing enterocolitis, or perforation (bilious vomiting, bloody stools, distension)

findings.text: Pneumatosis intestinalis or free air suggesting necrotizing enterocolitis or perforation

imaging.preferred_when: Respiratory distress, apnea, or cyanosis suggesting pneumonia, respiratory distress syndrome, or cardiac disease

findings.text: Clear lungs with normal cardiac silhouette
Focal or diffuse opacities suggesting pneumonia
Ground-glass opacities and low lung volumes suggesting respiratory distress syndrome

initial.why: Bedside glucose is checked in every irritable or jittery newborn; hypoglycemia is a common, immediately treatable mimic of withdrawal
Looks for infection or anemia that could explain irritability, poor feeding and lethargy
Assesses hydration, electrolytes, glucose and acid-base status in an infant with vomiting, diarrhea and poor intake
Hypocalcemia causes jitteriness, tremor and seizures and mimics withdrawal
Hypomagnesemia often accompanies hypocalcemia and can cause similar neurologic signs
Documents in utero substance exposure and identifies the agent, which guides monitoring and treatment
initial.only_if: maternal substance use is known or suspected

initial.why: Confirms the agent and timing of exposure when the history is incomplete or unclear
initial.only_if: maternal substance use is known or suspected

supporting.why: Supports or argues against infection when the infant is irritable, feeding poorly or has temperature instability
Screens for poor perfusion or metabolic derangement in a lethargic or unstable infant
Evaluates for an inborn error of metabolism when vomiting, lethargy or poor feeding are prominent
supporting.only_if: metabolic disease is suspected (lethargy, vomiting, acidosis, or a normal drug screen)

supporting.why: Newborn screen already covers congenital hypothyroidism; repeat only if the screen is unavailable or abnormal
supporting.only_if: newborn screen is unavailable or abnormal

supporting.why: Evaluates for intracranial hemorrhage or injury when seizures or focal neurologic signs are present
Characterizes brain injury when seizures or focal findings are not explained by ultrasound
supporting.only_if: seizures or focal neurologic findings persist

not_indicated.why: Not routine; lungs are normal in uncomplicated withdrawal
not_indicated.only_if: respiratory distress, apnea or cyanosis suggests pneumonia or respiratory disease

not_indicated.why: Not routine; loose stools alone do not require imaging
not_indicated.only_if: bilious vomiting, bloody stools, distension or suspected obstruction or necrotizing enterocolitis

not_indicated.why: Lumbar puncture is not indicated for typical withdrawal; reserved for suspected meningitis or encephalitis
not_indicated.only_if: meningitis or encephalitis is suspected (fever, lethargy, bulging fontanelle, or seizures with infection concern)

not_indicated.why: Urinalysis is not part of the routine withdrawal workup

decision_points: Check bedside glucose in every irritable or jittery newborn before attributing symptoms to withdrawal
The diagnosis is clinical, based on maternal substance history and a standardized withdrawal scoring tool; drug testing supports but does not establish it
Treat nonpharmacologically first (swaddling, low-stimulation environment, frequent small feeds, skin-to-skin care) and add medication when scores are persistently high
Consider infection, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia and metabolic disease when symptoms are atypical, the drug screen is negative, or the infant is lethargic rather than irritable
Meconium or umbilical cord testing reflects later-pregnancy exposure and is more sensitive than urine when the history is uncertain

criteria.name: Clinical diagnosis of neonatal abstinence syndrome
criteria.summary: Diagnosis is made when an infant with known or suspected in utero substance exposure develops characteristic central nervous system, gastrointestinal and autonomic signs after birth, with symptom onset and severity depending on the substance and timing of last exposure. Standardized withdrawal scoring tools quantify severity and guide treatment; drug testing supports the diagnosis but a negative test does not exclude it.
items: Maternal history of opioid or other substance use during pregnancy, including prescribed methadone or buprenorphine
Onset of symptoms after birth (typically 24–72 hours for short-acting opioids, up to 5–7 days for methadone or buprenorphine)
Central nervous system signs such as high-pitched cry, tremor, irritability, hypertonia or seizures
Gastrointestinal signs such as poor feeding, vomiting or diarrhea
Autonomic signs such as sweating, yawning, sneezing or nasal stuffiness
Symptoms not better explained by infection, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, metabolic disease or neurologic injury

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: An irritable, poorly feeding newborn with temperature instability and vomiting can look like withdrawal, and both are common in the same population.
differential.trigger: Fever or temperature instability, lethargy, poor perfusion, or respiratory distress in a newborn

history: Maternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, or group B streptococcus colonization
Onset within the first 24 hours of life
Infant is lethargic rather than jittery and irritable
exam: Poor perfusion, mottling, or delayed capillary refill
Lethargy or poor responsiveness
Respiratory distress with grunting, retractions, or apnea
labs: Elevated CRP or abnormal CBC with left shift
imaging: Chest x-ray with focal or diffuse opacities if pneumonia is present

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Low blood glucose causes jitteriness, tremor, irritability, poor feeding and even seizures, closely mimicking withdrawal.
differential.trigger: Jitteriness or tremor in a newborn, especially if the infant is also lethargic or feeding poorly

history: Infant of a diabetic mother, small for gestational age, large for gestational age, or preterm
Symptoms improve after feeding or glucose administration
No maternal opioid or substance use history
exam: Jitteriness that may be suppressed by gentle restraint
Lethargy or poor responsiveness between episodes
Symptoms resolve quickly after glucose correction
labs: Low bedside glucose (typically below 40–45 mg/dL in a symptomatic newborn)
Resolution of symptoms with glucose correction

differential.name: Hypocalcemia
differential.why_considered: Low calcium causes jitteriness, tremor, hyperreflexia and seizures that are difficult to distinguish from withdrawal on exam alone.
differential.trigger: Tremor, jitteriness or seizures in a newborn, especially after a complicated delivery or in an infant of a diabetic mother

history: Preterm birth, infant of a diabetic mother, or perinatal asphyxia
Symptoms may begin in the first 24–48 hours
No maternal substance use history
exam: Jitteriness and hyperreflexia
Seizures that may be subtle or focal
Symptoms improve with calcium replacement

differential.name: Infantile colic
differential.why_considered: Paroxysmal inconsolable crying in an otherwise well infant can be mistaken for withdrawal, especially when the maternal history is not known.

history: Crying episodes cluster in the evening and begin around 2–3 weeks of age
Infant is otherwise feeding and gaining weight well
No maternal substance use history
exam: Normal tone, reflexes and neurologic exam
Infant is consolable between episodes
No tremor, sweating, or gastrointestinal signs

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux
differential.why_considered: Frequent spitting up, irritability with feeds and poor weight gain overlap with the gastrointestinal features of withdrawal.

history: Symptoms mainly after feeds, not continuous
No maternal substance use history
No tremor, sweating or high-pitched cry
exam: Normal neurologic exam without tremor or hypertonia
Infant consolable and gaining weight

differential.name: Intracranial hemorrhage
differential.why_considered: A newborn with irritability, seizures, poor feeding and a high-pitched cry may have intracranial bleeding rather than withdrawal.
differential.trigger: Seizures, a bulging fontanelle, or focal neurologic findings in a newborn

history: Difficult or traumatic delivery, instrumented delivery, or prematurity
Seizures or lethargy rather than jitteriness
No maternal substance use history
exam: Bulging or tense fontanelle
Focal neurologic deficits or asymmetric findings
Lethargy or poor responsiveness
imaging: Cranial ultrasound showing germinal matrix, intraventricular or parenchymal hemorrhage
MRI brain confirming hemorrhage or ischemic injury

differential.name: Inborn error of metabolism
differential.why_considered: Metabolic disorders can present in the newborn period with vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, irritability and seizures, mimicking withdrawal.
differential.trigger: Vomiting, lethargy, acidosis or a negative drug screen in an irritable newborn

history: Symptoms worsen with feeding or after a period of apparent wellness
Consanguinity or a family history of infant deaths
No maternal substance use history
exam: Lethargy or poor responsiveness
Vomiting and dehydration
Abnormal odor or dysmorphic features in some disorders
labs: Metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap

differential.name: Maternal SSRI exposure (poor neonatal adaptation)
differential.why_considered: Late-pregnancy SSRI exposure can cause jitteriness, irritability, poor feeding and respiratory signs that resemble mild withdrawal.

history: Maternal SSRI use in the third trimester
Symptoms begin within the first few days and are usually milder and shorter than opioid withdrawal
No maternal opioid use
exam: Mild jitteriness and irritability
Usually no marked gastrointestinal signs or high-pitched cry
Symptoms resolve over days to a couple of weeks

severity.mild: Mild jitteriness and irritability that is consolable with swaddling and feeding; minimal gastrointestinal or autonomic signs; feeding and weight gain are preserved.
severity.moderate: Persistent irritability with high-pitched cry, tremor, increased tone and feeding difficulties; vomiting and loose stools; requires nonpharmacologic care and often medication.
severity.severe: Marked inconsolable irritability, hypertonia, exaggerated reflexes, poor feeding with dehydration, and possible seizures; requires medication and close monitoring.
severity.critical: Exhaustion or lethargy between episodes of extreme irritability, dehydration, inadequate feeding, and seizures; risk of aspiration, respiratory compromise or electrolyte derangement.

red_flags.meaning: Severe withdrawal or another serious cause such as hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, intracranial hemorrhage or infection; requires immediate evaluation and treatment.
Suggests sepsis, metabolic disease, hypoglycemia or another diagnosis rather than uncomplicated withdrawal.
Raises concern for neonatal sepsis, which must be evaluated and treated.

red_flags.finding: Poor feeding with dehydration or weight loss
red_flags.meaning: Risk of hypoglycemia, electrolyte disturbance and failure to thrive; may require intravenous fluids and nutritional support.
Suggests pneumonia, respiratory distress syndrome, cardiac disease or sepsis rather than withdrawal alone.

red_flags.finding: Bulging fontanelle or focal neurologic deficit
red_flags.meaning: Suggests intracranial hemorrhage, meningitis or another structural cause.

complications.name: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance
clues: Sunken fontanelle or decreased urine output

complications.name: Failure to thrive and poor weight gain
Seizures
clues: Subtle, focal or generalized seizure activity
Occurs with severe withdrawal or another metabolic or neurologic cause

complications.name: Neurodevelopmental and behavioral problems
clues: Long-term follow-up showing attention, behavior or developmental concerns
Often confounded by social and environmental factors

special_populations.differences: Preterm infants may show less severe withdrawal with fewer gastrointestinal symptoms and more subtle neurologic signs; symptoms may be delayed. Infants exposed to benzodiazepines or barbiturates may have a later onset and more seizures.

Maternal opioid use in pregnancy is managed with methadone or buprenorphine rather than withdrawal, because withdrawal risks fetal loss; the newborn should be monitored for abstinence syndrome after delivery.

key_questions.question: Did you use opioids, or any other drugs, during pregnancy — including prescribed methadone or buprenorphine?
key_questions.looking_for: Any opioid or other substance exposure in utero, including medication-assisted treatment, which is the key exposure for withdrawal

key_questions.question: When was your last dose of opioid or other substance before delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Timing of last exposure; short-acting opioids cause symptoms within 24–72 hours, methadone or buprenorphine up to 5–7 days

key_questions.question: When did the baby start to seem jittery or irritable?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset after birth, typically within the first few days; helps distinguish withdrawal from other causes

key_questions.question: How is the baby feeding, and is there spitting up or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, vomiting, loose stools — gastrointestinal features of withdrawal and risk for dehydration

key_questions.question: Does the baby have a high-pitched cry or trouble sleeping?
key_questions.looking_for: High-pitched cry and irritability that is difficult to console, classic central nervous system signs

key_questions.question: Does the baby sweat, yawn, sneeze, or have a stuffy nose?
Has the baby had any shaking spells or seizures?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, which indicate severe withdrawal or another serious cause such as hypoglycemia or hypocalcemia

key_questions.question: Did you have prenatal care, and were any infections or complications found during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Limited prenatal care, congenital infections, or other risk factors common in this population

key_questions.question: What other medicines, including antidepressants, benzodiazepines, or gabapentin, did you take during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Additional exposures that can cause or worsen withdrawal, such as SSRIs, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates

key_questions.question: Was the baby born early or at term, and how was the delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth (often less severe withdrawal) or a difficult delivery suggesting other causes of neurologic signs

key_questions.question: Has the baby had a fever, been lethargic, or had trouble breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Features that argue against uncomplicated withdrawal and suggest sepsis, metabolic disease, or another diagnosis

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of metabolic disease or infant deaths?
key_questions.looking_for: Inborn errors of metabolism that can mimic withdrawal
